div.head: 389. Intelligence Memorandum Prepared in the Central Intelligence Agency
div.p: ECUADOR: The Febres-Cordero Administration and Its Challenges

During his first one and a half years in office, President Leon Febres-Cordero has demonstrated forceful, often controversial, leadership in implementing conservative policies that frequently have been closely aligned with US interests. He has been especially vigorous in his efforts to reorient and revive the economy. His market-oriented strategies achieved early positive results in both the external accounts and domestic recovery, but the rapid decline in world market prices for oil—Ecuador’s chief foreign exchange earner—now threatens to reverse many of the gains. Febres-Cordero has also launched a dedicated and successful drug enforcement campaign. He has had frequent battles with the legislature over his efforts to expand presidential powers—resulting in charges that he has dictatorial tendencies—and a recent military mutiny tainted his administration with accusations of corruption. His efforts to counter the terrorist activities of the fledgling guerrilla organization, Alfaro Vive Carajo, have lately met with some success due to police penetrations, but he faces growing opposition from leftist political groups likely to win seats in the 1 June Congressional elections.
[Omitted here is the body of paper.]

note.p: Source: Central Intelligence Agency, Office of Support Services (DI), Job 86T01017R: Intell Publications Files (1985–87), Box 7, Folder 716: ALA M 86–20017. Secret; Noforn; [handling restriction not declassified]. Prepared for Casey in the South America Division, Office of African and Latin American Analysis and coordinated with DO. Based on information available as of April 23.

The New York Times reported that on March 14: “About 2,000 soldiers, backed by tanks and artillery, today recaptured a Quito air base held by the former armed forces Chief of Staff, who had called for the overthrow of the President. A Government spokesman said the rebel leader, Frank Vargas Pazos, had been captured.” Vargas first “rebelled March 7, taking over the air base in the coastal city of Manta, after Mr. Febres Cordero dismissed him for demanding the resignation and imprisonment of the Defense Minister and the army commander, whom he had accused of misuse of public funds. Defense Minister Luis Pineiros and Gen. Manuel Albuja, the army commander, resigned on Tuesday. Mr. Vargas surrendered that night and was taken from Manta to the base in Quito, saying he had the President’s ‘word of honor’ that he would be tried by a military court. But on Thursday, Mr. Vargas was freed by sympathetic officers and he took over the Quito base, asserting that the Government had broken the surrender agreement.” (“Ecuador Rebels Routed And Leader Is Captured,” New York Times, March 15, 1986, p. 3) In a March 14 memorandum drafted by Gelbard for Shultz’s meeting that day with Reagan, Gelbard wrote: “It was clear that Febres-Cordero had to act decisively in the face of Vargas’s ‘declaration of war’ against Febres, since he was already being seen as indecisive in the way he handled the first Vargas confrontation.” (Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 4B, 1986 Latin America) According to the President’s Daily Diary, Shultz and Poindexter met with Reagan on March 14 from 1:31 to 2:08 p.m. (Reagan Library, President’s Daily Diary)

In telegram 3012 from Quito, April 3, the Embassy reported that Febres-Cordero had said that day that the military crisis led by rebel Air Force General Frank Vargas “represented 3 coup attempts. Two came from Vargas who wanted to overthrow the government and the other from the military who wanted Febres Cordero to assume dictatorial powers. Febres Cordero told his Army commanders that he would go home before violating his constitutional oath. He ordered the Army to subdue Vargas or replace him as President. The Army opted to support the constitutional order and Febres Cordero states democracy emerged strengthened in Ecuador.” (Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Country File, Ecuador (03/24/1986–01/15/1987))
